reference.source: Standard vascular surgery reference texts and visceral aneurysm consensus guidance
clinicalPearls: The most common visceral artery aneurysm, frequently found incidentally on cross-sectional imaging as a calcified lesion near the splenic hilum
There is a marked female predominance, and multiparity and pregnancy are important associations
Portal hypertension and cirrhosis substantially increase both prevalence and size of these aneurysms
Most are asymptomatic, but larger or symptomatic lesions may cause left upper quadrant or epigastric pain
Rupture is the feared complication and can present as a two-stage bleed, initially contained within the lesser sac before free intraperitoneal haemorrhage
Rupture risk is especially high in pregnancy, where it carries grave maternal and fetal mortality, and this drives aggressive treatment in women of childbearing potential
Repair, by endovascular embolisation or open or laparoscopic surgery, is generally advised for large, symptomatic, or pregnancy-associated aneurysms
reference.pathophysiology: A splenic artery aneurysm is a focal dilatation of the splenic artery caused by weakening of the arterial wall, with degeneration of elastic and muscular layers and medial fibrodysplasia. Hormonal and haemodynamic changes of pregnancy, portal hypertension with increased splenic blood flow, atherosclerosis and fibromuscular dysplasia all contribute to wall stress and progressive enlargement. As the aneurysm grows, wall tension rises and the risk of rupture increases; rupture may initially be tamponaded within the lesser sac, producing transient stability before catastrophic free intraperitoneal haemorrhage and haemodynamic collapse.
additionalDifferentials: Splenic artery pseudoaneurysm (often post-pancreatitis or trauma)
Other visceral artery aneurysms (hepatic, coeliac, gastroduodenal)
additionalInvestigations: Contrast-enhanced CT angiography to confirm and size the aneurysm and assess its relation to the splenic hilum
Doppler ultrasound for detection and surveillance, particularly in pregnancy where radiation is avoided
MR angiography as a radiation-sparing alternative for characterisation and follow-up
Catheter angiography when endovascular treatment is planned
Assessment for portal hypertension and liver disease as underlying drivers
Serial imaging surveillance of small asymptomatic aneurysms to monitor growth
redFlags: Sudden severe abdominal pain with hypotension suggesting rupture
A two-stage presentation with transient stabilisation before collapse
Rapidly enlarging or large aneurysm on serial imaging
Any splenic artery aneurysm identified in a pregnant patient given the high rupture-related mortality
reference.prognosis: Unruptured aneurysms treated electively have an excellent outcome, whereas rupture carries high mortality, particularly in pregnancy; elective repair of high-risk lesions therefore markedly improves prognosis, and small low-risk aneurysms can be safely surveyed.
pitfalls: Dismissing an incidental calcified splenic lesion without appreciating rupture risk in higher-risk groups
Underestimating the danger of even modest-sized aneurysms during pregnancy
Confusing a true aneurysm with a post-inflammatory pseudoaneurysm, which has different management urgency
Failing to identify and address underlying portal hypertension
references: Rutherford's Vascular Surgery and Endovascular Therapy
Society for Vascular Surgery guidance on visceral artery aneurysms
management: Elective repair of aneurysms meeting treatment criteria (symptomatic, enlarging, or in women of childbearing potential) rather than watchful waiting, given rupture risk
Endovascular treatment with coil embolisation or a covered stent as preferred first-line intervention, with open ligation, aneurysmectomy or splenectomy where anatomy is unfavourable
Surveillance imaging with Doppler ultrasound or CT or MR angiography for small asymptomatic aneurysms to monitor growth
Aggressive treatment in pregnancy, and pre-conception counselling, given the grave maternal and foetal mortality of rupture
Address underlying drivers, particularly portal hypertension and chronic liver disease
Emergency resuscitation with urgent operative or endovascular control for rupture presenting with intraperitoneal haemorrhage
Cardiovascular risk factor modification where atherosclerotic disease coexists
